issues.title: `read_ipc` panics (`cast_slice>TargetAlignmentGreaterAndInputNotAligned`) on a compressed IPC file whose Decimal128 buffer is stored uncompressed (length -1)
issues.body:
### Checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pypi.org/project/polars/) of Polars.

### Reproducible example

The file below is the output of `clickhouse local -q "SELECT toDecimal64(1.5, 2) AS c FORMAT Arrow" > dec.arrow` (ClickHouse 26.11, default LZ4_FRAME compression), embedded as base64 (506 bytes):

```python
import base64, io
import polars as pl
import pyarrow as pa

data = base64.b64decode(
    "QVJST1cxAAD/////gAAAABAAAAAAAAoADAAGAAUACAAKAAAAAAEEABAAAAAMAAwAAAAEAAAACAAMAAAAFAAAAAQA"
    "AAABAAAAAgAAAAAAAAABAAAAEAAAAAwAEAAIAAAABwAMAAwAAAAAAAAHCAAAABQAAAABAAAAYwAAAAgADAAEAAgA"
    "CAAAABIAAAACAAAA/////5gAAAAUAAAAAAAAAAwAGAAGAAUACAAMAAwAAAAAAwQAHAAAABgAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAwA"
    "HAAQAAQACAAMAAwAAABAAAAAFAAAAFAAAAABAAAAAAAAAAAAAAACAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA"
    "GAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAQAAAAEAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAEAAQABAAAAP//////////lgAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAABAA"
    "AAAMABQABgAIAAwAEAAMAAAAAAAEADgAAAAkAAAABAAAAAEAAACQAAAAAAAAAKAAAAAAAAAAGAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA"
    "DAAMAAAABAAAAAgADAAAABQAAAAEAAAAAQAAAAIAAAAAAAAAAQAAABAAAAAMABAACAAAAAcADAAMAAAAAAAABwgA"
    "AAAUAAAAAQAAAGMAAAAIAAwABAAIAAgAAAASAAAAAgAAAKgAAABBUlJPVzE="
)
print(pa.ipc.open_file(pa.BufferReader(data)).read_all().to_pylist())
print(pl.read_ipc(io.BytesIO(data)))
```

Output:

```
[{'c': Decimal('1.50')}]
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File ".../polars/io/ipc/functions.py", line 203, in read_ipc
    return lf._collect_eager()
  ...
pyo3_runtime.PanicException: called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: JoinError::Panic(Id(37), "cast_slice>TargetAlignmentGreaterAndInputNotAligned", ...)
```


### Log output

```shell
The application panicked (crashed).
Message:  cast_slice>TargetAlignmentGreaterAndInputNotAligned
Location: .../bytemuck-1.25.2/src/internal.rs:33

with RUST_BACKTRACE=1:
  11: cast_slice<u8, i128>
  13: read_compressed_buffer<i128, core::io::cursor::Cursor<&[u8]>>
      at crates/polars-arrow/src/io/ipc/read/read_basic.rs:144
      at crates/polars-arrow/src/io/ipc/read/read_basic.rs:253
      at crates/polars-arrow/src/io/ipc/read/array/primitive.rs:43
```

### Issue description


The file is a valid Arrow IPC file: the record batch has `BodyCompression` LZ4_FRAME, and the 16-byte Decimal128 data buffer is stored uncompressed with the length prefix `-1`, which the format allows ("The uncompressed length may be set to -1 to indicate that the data that follows is not compressed"). Arrow C++ writes such buffers when `IpcWriteOptions::min_space_savings` is set and compression does not save enough (arrow-go has `WithMinSpaceSavings`); ClickHouse's `Arrow` output format does it for small buffers, as here. pyarrow reads the file. Polars panics in `pl.read_ipc`, `pl.scan_ipc(...).collect()` and (for the `ArrowStream` variant of the same output) `pl.read_ipc_stream`. ZSTD files behave the same.

It happens for any Decimal column (ClickHouse writes Decimal32/64/128 as Arrow `decimal128`) as long as the buffer is stored with `-1`; with 1000 rows ClickHouse compresses the buffer and the file reads fine. Int64 and other 8-byte columns in the same situation read fine.

Cause: the `-1` branch of `read_compressed_buffer` (added in #24674) in [`crates/polars-arrow/src/io/ipc/read/read_basic.rs#L143-L145`](https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/blob/c706e7ebe8b6422679b37e46fbe6026cb46a9a7c/crates/polars-arrow/src/io/ipc/read/read_basic.rs#L143-L145):

```rust
if decompressed_len_field == -1 {
    return Ok(bytemuck::cast_slice(&scratch[8..]).to_vec());
}
```

`scratch` is a `Vec<u8>`, so its start is at best 16-byte aligned and `&scratch[8..]` is only 8-byte aligned. For `T = i128` (alignment 16), `bytemuck::cast_slice` panics. The compressed branch decompresses into a `Vec<T>` and is not affected. Copying instead of casting, for example `bytemuck::pod_collect_to_vec::<u8, T>(&scratch[8..])`, would fix it (the `row_limit` that the compressed branch applies is also ignored on this path).

#14215 (open) reported the earlier failure on `-1` buffers (`LZ4 error: ERROR_frameType_unknown`); the file attached there (a `uint8` column) now reads correctly on main, so that issue could probably be closed. This report is the remaining case for 16-byte types.

Tested on main c706e7ebe8b6422679b37e46fbe6026cb46a9a7c (2026-10-18, built from source) and on the 2.0.0 wheel from PyPI: same panic.


### Expected behavior


```
shape: (1, 1)
┌───────────────┐
│ c             │
│ ---           │
│ decimal[18,2] │
╞═══════════════╡
│ 1.50          │
└───────────────┘
```

as with `pl.read_ipc(io.BytesIO(data), use_pyarrow=True)`, which prints this.

issues.title: `write_csv` / `write_ndjson` round the UTC offset of a tz-aware Datetime to whole minutes, so timestamps in zones with second-level offsets are written up to 30 s off
issues.body:
### Checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pypi.org/project/polars/) of Polars.

### Reproducible example

```python

```
```python
import io
from datetime import datetime
import polars as pl

utc = pl.Series("ts", [datetime(1960, 6, 1, 12)], dtype=pl.Datetime("us", "UTC"))
df = pl.DataFrame({"ts": utc.dt.convert_time_zone("Africa/Monrovia")})  # UTC offset then: -00:44:30
print(df)

csv = df.write_csv()
ndjson = df.write_ndjson()
print(csv, ndjson, sep="")
print(pl.read_csv(io.StringIO(csv), schema={"ts": pl.Datetime("us", "UTC")})["ts"][0])
print(pl.read_ndjson(io.StringIO(ndjson), schema={"ts": pl.Datetime("us", "UTC")})["ts"][0])
```

Output:

```
shape: (1, 1)
┌───────────────────────────────┐
│ ts                            │
│ ---                           │
│ datetime[μs, Africa/Monrovia] │
╞═══════════════════════════════╡
│ 1960-06-01 11:15:30 MMT       │
└───────────────────────────────┘
ts
1960-06-01T11:15:30.000000-0045
{"ts":"1960-06-01T11:15:30-00:45"}

1960-06-01 12:00:30+00:00
1960-06-01 12:00:30+00:00
```


### Log output

```shell

```

### Issue description


The stored instant is 12:00:00 UTC. Polars writes the local wall time with the exact offset (`11:15:30` = 12:00:00 - 0:44:30) but prints the offset rounded to whole minutes (`-0045` / `-00:45`), so the text in the file denotes 12:00:30 UTC, and reading the file back yields a timestamp 30 s later. No error or warning.

This affects every timestamp at which the zone's UTC offset is not a whole number of minutes, e.g. Africa/Monrovia before 1972 (+30 s), Europe/Dublin before 1916 (-21 s), Europe/Paris before 1911 (+21 s), America/New_York before 1883 (LMT -4:56:02, -2 s), and the LMT period of every zone. `write_json` and the `Datetime` -> `String` cast (`1960-06-01 11:15:30.000000-00:45`) do the same; because the cast is also used for hive partition paths, `write_parquet(partition_by=...)` on such a key writes `k=1960-06-01%2011%3A15%3A30.000000-00%3A45` and the key is read back 30 s off. Parquet/IPC columns are not affected (they store UTC).

Cause (main 0b61a868): `crates/polars-io/src/csv/write/write_impl.rs` formats zoned datetimes with the default `"%FT%H:%M:%S.%3f%z"` / `%6f%z` / `%9f%z`, and `crates/polars-json/src/json/write/serialize.rs` uses chrono's `to_rfc3339()`. Both compute the wall time with the full offset but print `%z` / RFC 3339 offsets, which have no seconds field. `%::z` (which `dt.to_string("%FT%T%::z")` already supports: `1960-06-01T11:15:30-00:44:30`) would be lossless, but `read_csv` currently cannot parse an offset with seconds (`could not find a 'date/datetime' pattern`), so falling back to UTC (or `Z`) for such values may be the simpler fix.

Tested on main 0b61a868d644d31ddadc05001b581bb66d3b8665 (2026-10-17, built from source) and on the 2.0.0 wheel from PyPI: identical output.


### Expected behavior

The written text should denote the stored instant, e.g. `1960-06-01T11:15:30.000000-00:44:30` or `1960-06-01T12:00:00.000000+0000`, and reading the file back should give `1960-06-01 12:00:00+00:00`.

comments.body:
I'd like to take this one on, following the contributing guide — I went straight to a PR (#29890) before commenting here, which is my mistake and why @orlp closed it.

issues.body:
### Checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pypi.org/project/polars/) of Polars.

### Reproducible example

This one is super short,

```python
import polars as pl
import numpy as np
pl.from_dicts([{'a': np.array(1)}])
```


### Log output

```shell
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../type_error.py", line 3, in <module>
    pl.from_dicts([{'a': np.array(1)}])
  File "/home/username/bin/venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/polars/convert/general.py", line 218, in from_dicts
    return pl.DataFrame(
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/home/username/bin/venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/polars/dataframe/frame.py", line 417, in __init__
    self._df = sequence_to_pydf(
               ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/home/username/bin/venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/polars/_utils/construction/dataframe.py", line 470, in sequence_to_pydf
    return to_pydf(
           ^^^^^^^^
  File "/home/username/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.12.13-linux-x86_64-gnu/lib/python3.12/functools.py", line 912, in wrapper
    return dispatch(args[0].__class__)(*args, **kw)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/home/username/bin/venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/polars/_utils/construction/dataframe.py", line 728, in _sequence_of_dict_to_pydf
    pydf = PyDataFrame.from_dicts(
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: len() of unsized object
```

### Issue description

Happens on latest version 2.0.0 and 1.44.2

### Expected behavior

Should work similarly to pl.from_dicts([{'a': 1}]), but with numpy type of scalar (behavior here: int64); if sweeping multiple dicts and types mismatch, then I think reasonable behavior match what happens with arrays, which seems to be type promotion (ints to floats, numeric and string to string).

```
In [1]: import numpy as np, polars as pl
   ...: pl.from_dicts([{'a': np.array([1, 2])}, {'a': np.array([3.5, 4.5])}])   # int64 vs float64 arrays
   ...: 
Out[1]: 
shape: (2, 1)
┌────────────┐
│ a          │
│ ---        │
│ list[f64]  │
╞════════════╡
│ [1.0, 2.0] │
│ [3.5, 4.5] │
└────────────┘

In [2]: pl.from_dicts([{'a': np.array([1, 2])}, {'a': np.array(['x', 'y'])}])   # int64 vs str arrays
Out[2]: 
shape: (2, 1)
┌────────────┐
│ a          │
│ ---        │
│ list[str]  │
╞════════════╡
│ ["1", "2"] │
│ ["x", "y"] │
└────────────┘
```

Regarding other constructors

Works:
- `pl.DataFrame([(np.array(1),)], schema={'a': pl.Int64})` - 0-d array coerced to scalar when schema given.
- `pl.from_records([(np.array(1),)], schema={'a': pl.Int64})` - same.
- `pl.Series('a', np.array(1))` - 0-d array passed directly is treated as a scalar value → `i64`.
- `pl.DataFrame([{'a': np.int64(1)}])` - numpy scalars work.

Same bug (`TypeError: len() of unsized object` — a bare `len()` call on a 0-d array, which has no `__len__`):
- `pl.from_dicts([{'a': np.array(1)}])` (original report)
- `pl.DataFrame({'a': np.array(1)})` - crashes in the multithreading heuristic (`len(val)`) before conversion even happens.
- `pl.Series('a', [np.array(1)])` - 0-d array *inside a list* crashes; inconsistent with `pl.Series('a', np.array(1))` which works.
- `pl.DataFrame([{'a': np.int64(1)}, {'a': np.array(1)}])` - crashes even when another row has a proper numpy scalar.
- `pl.DataFrame([{'a': np.array([1])}, {'a': np.array(1)}])` - crashes when mixed with a 1-d array.

### Description

Would a short Redis example or a link to the Redis driver's integration guide be appropriate in the database guide's ADBC section?

I maintain the community [Redis ADBC driver](https://github.com/alberttwong/redis-adbc-driver). Its Python package supports Polars' existing `read_database_uri(..., engine="adbc")` API. I propose documenting this integration so users can discover Redis as an ADBC data source.

Suggested example:

```python
import polars as pl

df = pl.read_database_uri(
    query="SELECT 1 AS one",
    uri="redis://localhost:6379/0",
    engine="adbc",
)
assert df.to_dicts() == [{"one": 1}]
```

Setup and scope:

- Python 3.10+; install Polars and the platform-specific Redis driver wheel with its `dbapi` extra from the [driver releases](https://github.com/alberttwong/redis-adbc-driver/releases). The wheels bundle the native driver and declare the ADBC manager/PyArrow dependencies. The package is not yet published to PyPI.
- For example, after downloading the matching wheel: `python -m pip install polars '/path/to/adbc_driver_redis-0.0.15-py3-none-<platform>.whl[dbapi]'`. Release v0.0.15 provides Linux x86_64/arm64 and macOS arm64 wheels.
- A running Redis instance with Search is required; the driver's recorded integration environment uses Redis 8.6.2 with Search. This is SQL provided by the external driver over Redis, rather than a native Redis SQL interface.
- The driver currently supports autocommit only. TLS connections use the `rediss://` scheme.

The repository includes a [Polars integration test](https://github.com/alberttwong/redis-adbc-driver/blob/main/python/tests/test_driver.py) and [recorded verification](https://github.com/alberttwong/redis-adbc-driver/blob/main/docs/sdlc/changes/271-280/validation.md) using Polars 2.0.0, ADBC manager 1.12.0, and PyArrow 26.0.0. The test checks the URI example above. I reran `test_dbapi_and_polars` on October 20, 2026, against a disposable `redis:8.6.2` container with those package versions: **1 passed** (macOS arm64, installed Python wheel with the locally built native library). [Installation and integration instructions](https://github.com/alberttwong/redis-adbc-driver/blob/main/docs/python-integrations.md) are available in the driver repository.

If this fits the documentation's scope, I can contribute a small documentation PR with either the example or a link, according to the maintainers' preferred placement.

### Link

https://docs.pola.rs/user-guide/io/database/#adbc

issues.title: SQL: `FROM` item aliases outlive the query and can replace registered tables
issues.body:
### Checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pypi.org/project/polars/) of Polars.

### Reproducible example

```python
import polars as pl

pl.DataFrame({"z": [7, 8]}).write_parquet("t.parquet")


def run(query: str) -> tuple[list[str], list[str]]:
    ctx = pl.SQLContext({"lineitem": pl.LazyFrame({"k": [1]})})
    ctx.execute(query).collect()
    return ctx.tables(), ctx.execute("SELECT * FROM lineitem").collect().columns


print(run("SELECT * FROM read_parquet('t.parquet') AS lineitem"))
print(run("SELECT * FROM UNNEST([1, 2]) AS lineitem(z)"))
print(run("SELECT * FROM (SELECT 5 AS z) AS lineitem"))
print(run("SELECT * FROM (SELECT 5 AS z) AS foo"))
```


### Log output

```shell
(['lineitem'], ['z'])         # registered `lineitem` replaced by the parquet file
(['lineitem'], ['z'])         # registered `lineitem` replaced by the UNNEST result
(['lineitem'], ['k'])         # derived table: not replaced (#29577)
(['foo', 'lineitem'], ['k'])  # derived table: added to the context
```

### Issue description

A relation introduced in a query's `FROM` outlives the query:

- Table functions (`read_parquet`, `read_csv`, ..., `range`, `generate_series`) and `UNNEST` write their result into the context under their alias (or name). A registered table with that name is replaced for all later queries.
- A derived table `(SELECT ...) AS foo` is added to the context when the name is free. #29577 stopped it from replacing a registered table; `test_cte_shadows_derived_table_from_earlier_query` asserts the persistence.

CTEs, by contrast, last for one statement. Postgres, DuckDB, SQLite, Spark and Trino scope all `FROM` items to their query; keeping a result takes `CREATE VIEW` or `CREATE TABLE ... AS`.

Possible directions:

1. Apply #29577 to table functions and `UNNEST`: visible for the statement, never replacing a registered table. Derived tables keep persisting when the name is free.
2. Scope all `FROM` items to their statement, like CTEs and other engines. This drops the derived-table persistence the test above asserts.

### Expected behavior

TBD - the alias should probably have a local scope and lifetime.

### Installed versions

Reproduces on 2.0.0 and latest main.

issues.title: Partitioned write puts a NULL key and the string "__HIVE_DEFAULT_PARTITION__" into the same file: rows silently lost, file sometimes unreadable
issues.body:
### Checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pypi.org/project/polars/) of Polars.

### Reproducible example


```python
import glob, shutil
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"p": [None, "__HIVE_DEFAULT_PARTITION__", None, "x"], "v": [1, 2, 3, 4]})

for run in range(10):
    shutil.rmtree("out", ignore_errors=True)
    df.write_parquet("out", partition_by="p")
    files = sorted(glob.glob("out/**/*.parquet", recursive=True))
    try:
        rows = pl.read_parquet("out/**/*.parquet", hive_partitioning=False)["v"].sort().to_list()
    except Exception as e:
        rows = f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}"
    print(run, files, rows)
```

Output (main):

```
0 ['out/p=__HIVE_DEFAULT_PARTITION__/00000000.parquet', 'out/p=x/00000000.parquet'] [2, 4]
1 ['out/p=__HIVE_DEFAULT_PARTITION__/00000000.parquet', 'out/p=x/00000000.parquet'] [2, 4]
2 ['out/p=__HIVE_DEFAULT_PARTITION__/00000000.parquet', 'out/p=x/00000000.parquet'] [2, 4]
3 ['out/p=__HIVE_DEFAULT_PARTITION__/00000000.parquet', 'out/p=x/00000000.parquet'] [2, 4]
4 ['out/p=__HIVE_DEFAULT_PARTITION__/00000000.parquet', 'out/p=x/00000000.parquet'] [2, 4]
5 ['out/p=__HIVE_DEFAULT_PARTITION__/00000000.parquet', 'out/p=x/00000000.parquet'] ComputeError: parquet: File out of specification: Unexpected struct field type 15
6 ['out/p=__HIVE_DEFAULT_PARTITION__/00000000.parquet', 'out/p=x/00000000.parquet'] [2, 4]
7 ['out/p=__HIVE_DEFAULT_PARTITION__/00000000.parquet', 'out/p=x/00000000.parquet'] ComputeError: parquet: File out of specification: Unexpected struct field type 15
8 ['out/p=__HIVE_DEFAULT_PARTITION__/00000000.parquet', 'out/p=x/00000000.parquet'] [2, 4]
9 ['out/p=__HIVE_DEFAULT_PARTITION__/00000000.parquet', 'out/p=x/00000000.parquet'] [2, 4]
```

The streaming sink behaves the same: `df.lazy().sink_parquet(pl.PartitionBy("out2", key="p"), mkdir=True)` repeated 30 times left `out2/p=__HIVE_DEFAULT_PARTITION__/00000000.parquet` with 1 row 23 times, 2 rows once and an unreadable file 6 times (never the expected 3 rows).


### Log output

```shell
polars.exceptions.ComputeError: parquet: File out of specification: Unexpected struct field type 15
```

### Issue description


4 rows are written, but only 2 are on disk (in some runs 3: the two NULL rows win and the `"__HIVE_DEFAULT_PARTITION__"` row is lost), or a corrupt file, and the write returns without an error.

The NULL key and the string key `"__HIVE_DEFAULT_PARTITION__"` are two different partitions, but they are rendered to the same directory `p=__HIVE_DEFAULT_PARTITION__/`, and both partitions' first file is `00000000.parquet`. The writer opens the same path twice: the partitions overwrite each other, and when the two writes interleave the result is a Parquet file with a broken footer that no reader can open.

Cause (main 0b61a868): `HivePathFormatter::fmt` (`crates/polars-io/src/hive.rs`) writes a NULL key as the bare text `__HIVE_DEFAULT_PARTITION__` and percent-encodes non-null values with `HIVE_VALUE_ENCODE_CHARSET` (`crates/polars-io/src/utils/mod.rs`), which leaves that text unchanged; `HivePathProvider::get_path` (`crates/polars-plan/src/dsl/options/file_provider.rs`) then appends `{index_in_partition:08x}.parquet`, so both partitions get the identical path. Nothing checks for duplicate paths.

For comparison, pyarrow `write_dataset(..., partitioning=['p'], partitioning_flavor='hive')` writes both groups into one `p=__HIVE_DEFAULT_PARTITION__/part-0.parquet` and keeps all 4 rows.

Related but different: #26885 (custom file provider returning duplicate paths), #18242 (overwriting files from an earlier write).

Tested on main 0b61a868d644d31ddadc05001b581bb66d3b8665 (2026-10-17, built from source) and on the 2.0.0 wheel from PyPI (same loss, also an unreadable file in 2 to 6 of 30 runs).


### Expected behavior

All 4 rows are on disk after the write, e.g. by escaping a string value that equals the null sentinel (e.g. `%5F_HIVE_DEFAULT_PARTITION__`) so that the two partitions get different directories. At minimum the writer should raise instead of writing two partitions to the same file.


### Installed versions


<details>

```

Build:               <unknown>
Index type:          UInt32
Platform:            Linux-5.15.0-187-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.35
Python:              3.12.15 (main, Oct 14 2026, 01:05:27) [Clang 23.1.3 ]
Runtime:             rt32

comments.body: Sorry, you put `__HIVE_DEFAULT_PARTITION__` as a value in your DataFrame? What did you expect? Do other tools support this?
comments.author: orlp

comments.body:
@orlp Fair question. The input is unusual, and I understand that the literal string conflicts with Hive’s null marker. I’m happy to drop the escaping suggestion.

My concern is that the write succeeds without an error but silently loses rows, and sometimes produces an unreadable Parquet file. Both partitions resolve to the same `00000000.parquet` path, so their writes can overwrite or interfere with each other. Even if this partition value is unsupported, I would expect an explicit error.

For comparison, in my PyArrow test, `write_dataset(..., partitioning=["p"], partitioning_flavor="hive")` writes both groups into one file and preserves all four rows, although that does not preserve the distinction between null and the literal string.

Either of these would address the overwrite/corruption issue:
1. If Hive semantics require treating these keys as equivalent, combine their rows safely.
2. Otherwise, raise an error when distinct partitions resolve to the same output path.

issues.title: Decimal32/Decimal64 values corrupted when imported via the generic Arrow C Stream PyCapsule path
issues.body:
### Checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pypi.org/project/polars/) of Polars.

### Reproducible example

```python
from decimal import Decimal
import pyarrow as pa
import polars as pl

class StreamOnly:
    """Wraps any __arrow_c_stream__ producer, but is NOT Iterable -- this
    forces pl.from_arrow through the generic PyCapsule import path instead
    of the pyarrow.Table/RecordBatch-specific handling (which is unaffected
    and gives correct results for the exact same data)."""
    def __init__(self, inner):
        self._inner = inner
    def __arrow_c_stream__(self, requested_schema=None):
        return self._inner.__arrow_c_stream__(requested_schema)

values = [Decimal("24.57900000"), Decimal("24.56725000"), Decimal("24.62450000"),
          Decimal("24.39175000"), Decimal("24.23350000")]
table = pa.table({"value": pa.array(values, type=pa.decimal64(18, 8))})
reader = pa.RecordBatchReader.from_batches(table.schema, table.to_batches())

print(pl.from_arrow(StreamOnly(reader)))
print("expected:", values)
```

### Log output

```shell
shape: (5,)
Series: '' [struct[1]]
[
	{453185773344840981962.75500000}
	{449948369759904955654.19250000}
	{24.23350000}
	{0.00000000}
	{0.00000000}
]
expected: [Decimal('24.57900000'), Decimal('24.56725000'), Decimal('24.62450000'), Decimal('24.39175000'), Decimal('24.23350000')]
```

### Issue description

Importing a `decimal64`/`decimal32` Arrow array through the generic Arrow C Stream PyCapsule path (any `__arrow_c_stream__` producer that isn't a `pyarrow.Table`/`RecordBatch`/`Array`/`ChunkedArray` -- these get redirected to pyarrow-specific handling in `from_arrow`, which is unaffected) silently corrupts the values instead of raising or returning the correct result.

The corrupted output follows a clear pattern: `result[i] = raw_unscaled[2*i] + raw_unscaled[2*i+1] * 2**64`, i.e. every pair of adjacent 8-byte decimal64 values is read as a single (wrong) 16-byte value, with an out-of-bounds read for the last element(s) when the count is odd. This means the physical buffer is being read with a 16-byte stride instead of the correct 8-byte stride for decimal64 (4-byte for decimal32).

I bisected this down to `to_physical_and_dtype` in `crates/polars-core/src/series/from.rs`, used when converting a `Struct`/`List`/`FixedSizeList` child to its physical representation (every Arrow C Stream record batch is exported as an implicit top-level `Struct`, so this path is hit for every column, not just nested ones). Its match on logical types that need conversion lists `ArrowDataType::Decimal(_, _)` (128-bit) but not `ArrowDataType::Decimal32`/`ArrowDataType::Decimal64`:

https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/blob/80b7a254534fccb80113231b69230131e00f12ac/crates/polars-core/src/series/from.rs#L838-L846

Since those two variants don't match any earlier arm either, they fall through to the generic catch-all a few lines below, which tags the array with the logical `DataType::Decimal(p, s)` *without* actually widening the physical buffer from 8/4 bytes to Polars' internal 16-byte (`i128`) decimal representation:

```rust
dt => {
    let dtype = DataType::from_arrow(dt, md);
    Ok((arrays, dtype))
},
```

Everything downstream then reads that buffer assuming 16-byte elements, producing the corruption above. I confirmed this by patching `polars-core`/`polars-arrow` locally (built against a `polars_arrow`/`polars_core` path dependency, bypassing the Python bindings) and adding `ArrowDataType::Decimal32(_, _) | ArrowDataType::Decimal64(_, _)` to that match arm's type list -- this fixes the reproduction above with correct output and no other observable change.

I also verified the buffer read at the raw FFI level (`polars_arrow::ffi::ArrowArrayStreamReader`) is byte-correct on its own -- the corruption is introduced specifically in this `polars-core` conversion step, not in the FFI import layer.

### Expected behavior

```
shape: (5,)
Series: '' [struct[1]]
[
	{24.57900000}
	{24.56725000}
	{24.62450000}
	{24.39175000}
	{24.23350000}
]
```

### Installed versions

Reproduces on `1.44.2` and `2.0.0-rc.2` (and on `main` at `da47b74`, verified by patching locally).

<details>

```

Build:               da47b7405f0e2d188e71cce7c2d588c695f4098d
Index type:          UInt32
Platform:            macOS-26.7-arm64-arm-64bit
Python:              3.10.16 (main, Feb 12 2025, 15:03:04) [Clang 19.1.6 ]
Runtime:             rt32

----Optional dependencies----

Unlike Decimal32/64 (silent corruption), Decimal256 hits an internal assertion and panics instead. Fix and a regression test covering all three widths are in #29652.

issues.title: Unnecessary multiplexing causes OOM with in-memory sources.
issues.body:
### Checks - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pypi.org/project/polars/) of Polars. ### Reproducible example Consider the following plan that computes the number of elements equal to the minimum value (and forget for a moment that this can be computed in streaming fashion with a specialized node, since the example applies to more general cases). ```python import polars as pl lf = pl.DataFrame({"x": range(100)}).lazy() plan = lf.select(pl.col("x").filter(pl.col("x") == pl.col("x").min()).count()) plan.show_graph(engine="streaming", plan_stage="physical") ``` Computationally, something like this requires two passes. One to compute the aggregation, and one that goes over the data once the aggregation is done. This is because it is impossible to know the value of the aggregation before all values are seen. Exceptions to this rule are aggregations such as `first()`, but it holds for most aggregations. The way polars plans this right now is by incorporating a multiplexer which is _potentially memory intensive_. ### Log output ```shell ``` ### Issue description I find there are two issues with this approach: First, the information is slightly misleading and could be stated better: the node is not _potentially memory intensive_. It is _definitely memory intensive_. The multiplexer will always need to hold all the data read. So this should be shown in red in the graph even though it runs in the streaming engine. Second, this should not run out of memory with in-memory sources. (Note that the fact that it is an in-memory-source does not mean that it fits in memory, since it can be a memory-mapped in-memory source.) Using multiplexers with in-memory sources are not a requirement because the data can be read multiple times. (In fact, multipass algorithms, which polars does not implement, are possible). Multiplexers in this case are only a potential optimization for improving cache access. In particular, when the data in one branch needs to see the full input to produce the result and the data in the other path cannot start computing before that branch is done, it is better to not have the multiplexer. ### Expected behavior There are two issues to solve. I think polars should properly display this plan with red nodes and I would like polars to optimize differently based on whether the data read can be read multiple times or not, such that this plan can run with constant memory for in-memory sources. ### Installed versions
``` --------Version info--------- Polars: 1.40.1 Index type: UInt32 Platform: Linux-6.8.0-110-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.35 Python: 3.12.12 (main, Feb 12 2026, 00:42:14) [Clang 21.1.4 ] Runtime: rt32 ----Optional dependencies---- Azure CLI adbc_driver_manager altair azure.identity boto3 cloudpickle connectorx deltalake fastexcel fsspec 2026.3.0 gevent google.auth great_tables matplotlib numpy 2.4.4 openpyxl pandas 3.0.2 polars_cloud pyarrow 23.0.1 pydantic 2.13.3 pyiceberg 0.11.1 sqlalchemy torch xlsx2csv xlsxwriter ```
issues.author: ramcasa

comments.body:
> First, the information is slightly misleading and could be stated better: the node is not potentially memory intensive. It is definitely memory intensive.

It's potentially memory intensive because those colorings only looks at a node in isolation. Whether a multiplexer is memory intensive or not depends on whether one of its output ports blocks indefinitely (which is the case for the `reduce` node). So that's not a bug.

> Second, this should not run out of memory with in-memory sources.

I agree, it's been on our radar for a while already that we want to split out trivial multiplexers into separate scans. Especially for in-memory sources the multiplexer doesn't really make sense.
comments.author: orlp

comments.body:
> It's potentially memory intensive because those colorings only looks at a node in isolation. Whether a multiplexer is memory intensive or not depends on whether one of its output ports blocks indefinitely (which is the case for the reduce node). So that's not a bug.

I understand that right now the mapping node to color only takes into account the node type. And sure, it's not a bug in that sense. But it's undersirable that, knowing that the plan is memory-intensive no matter the input data, this is not shown. Because I would expect that the colors mean:
* `white`: runs with fixed memory size in terms of the data schema.
* `yellow`: runs with a memory size footprint dependent on the data values. Potentially small if the data is "nice".
* `red`: it is forced to run with memory proportional to the length of the data.

So, more than a bugfix, I'm requesting a feature improvement: that the colors take into account global information, not just local.

> I agree, it's been on our radar for a while already that we want to split out trivial multiplexers into separate scans. Especially for in-memory sources the multiplexer doesn't really make sense.

Cool. That'd be great.
comments.author: ramcasa

comments.body: That would certainly be nice, but I don't think we have that information (`yellow` vs `red`) during planning.
comments.author: dsprenkels

comments.body:
We hit the same multiplexer issue with `.over()` on a streamed multi-file parquet scan (not just in-memory sources), and `set_sorted` on the partition key doesn't help — worth noting here since it's the unchecked `.over(keys)` → sorted-group-by item on #20947.

Toy repro: N parquet files, each already sorted by the group key `g` and disjoint across files, with a few float columns. Peak RSS grows linearly with input size for `.over()`, with or without `set_sorted`, and even for a hand-written sorted `group_by` + merge-join over the same scan:

| files (rows) | no window | `.over("g")` | `.over("g")` + `set_sorted("g")` | hand-written sorted `group_by` + merge-join | `.over("g")`, `POLARS_OOC_MEMORY_BUDGET_MB=1000` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 (40M)   | 1.37 GiB | 4.29 GiB | 4.17 GiB | 3.85 GiB | 3.84 GiB (6.8s vs 1.1s) |
| 16 (80M)  | 1.35 GiB | 6.90 GiB | 6.62 GiB | 6.59 GiB | 4.29 GiB (10.3s vs 1.5s) |
| 24 (120M) | 1.55 GiB | 9.65 GiB | 9.35 GiB | 9.20 GiB | 4.17 GiB (15.3s vs 2.2s) |

polars `2.0.0-rc.2`, `POLARS_MAX_THREADS=16`.

<details>
<summary>repro.py</summary>

```python
"""
.over(key) on a streamed multi-file parquet scan buffers the whole input.

polars 2.0.0-rc.2, POLARS_MAX_THREADS=16

Usage: python repro.py <no-window|over|over-sorted|gb-join-sorted> [n_files]
"""
import os
import resource
import sys
import time
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import polars as pl

DATA = Path(__file__).parent / "data"
ROWS_PER_FILE, GROUP_LEN, WIDE = 5_000_000, 400, 8


def gen(n_files):
    DATA.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    for f in range(n_files):
        n = ROWS_PER_FILE
        g = f * (n // GROUP_LEN) + np.arange(n) // GROUP_LEN  # sorted, disjoint per file
        cols = {"g": g.astype(np.int64), "k": (np.arange(n) % GROUP_LEN).astype(np.int32)}
        for i in range(WIDE):
            cols[f"v{i}"] = rng.standard_normal(n)
        pl.DataFrame(cols).write_parquet(DATA / f"part{f}.parquet", row_group_size=250_000)


def base(n_files):
    return pl.scan_parquet([DATA / f"part{f}.parquet" for f in range(n_files)])


AGGS = [
    pl.col("v0").max().over("g").alias("v0_max"),
    pl.col("v1").filter(pl.col("k") == 10).first().over("g").alias("v1_at10"),
    pl.col("v2").filter(pl.col("k") > 200).mean().over("g").alias("v2_mean"),
]
GB_AGGS = [
    pl.col("v0").max().alias("v0_max"),
    pl.col("v1").filter(pl.col("k") == 10).first().alias("v1_at10"),
    pl.col("v2").filter(pl.col("k") > 200).mean().alias("v2_mean"),
]


def build(variant, n_files):
    lf = base(n_files)
    if variant == "no-window":
        return lf
    if variant == "over":
        return lf.with_columns(AGGS)
    if variant == "over-sorted":
        return lf.set_sorted("g").with_columns(AGGS)
    if variant == "gb-join-sorted":  # hand-written sorted group_by + merge-join
        lf = lf.set_sorted("g")
        agg = lf.group_by("g", maintain_order=True).agg(GB_AGGS)
        return lf.join(agg, on="g", how="left")
    raise SystemExit(f"unknown variant {variant}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    variant = sys.argv[1]
    n_files = int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 8
    if not (DATA / f"part{n_files - 1}.parquet").exists():
        gen(n_files)
    plan = build(variant, n_files).select(pl.all().exclude("g", "k").sum())
    t = time.time()
    plan.collect(engine="streaming")
    rss_gib = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss / 2**20
    dt = time.time() - t
    ooc = os.environ.get("POLARS_OOC_MEMORY_BUDGET_MB", "-")
    print(f"{pl.__version__} files={n_files:3d} {variant:16s} OOC_MB={ooc:>6s} peak_rss={rss_gib:5.2f} GiB t={dt:5.1f}s")
```

</details>

- `.over(keys, mapping_strategy="group_to_rows")` always lowers to a hash `group_by` + left `EquiJoin` zipped against the original stream through a multiplexer (`try_build_streaming_group_by`, `GroupByLowerKind::Over` in `lower_expr.rs`). It never checks `are_keys_sorted_any` the way plain `IR::GroupBy` does in `lower_ir.rs`, so `set_sorted` on the key is a no-op here.
- Even hand-rolling the sorted path (sorted `group_by` + merge-join on the same sorted scan) grows the same way — the multiplexer has no backpressure between its branches, so the faster one just buffers ahead of the slower one regardless of node type.
- `POLARS_OOC_MEMORY_BUDGET_MB` keeps the peak flat at a real wall-time cost (~6-7x here). It's off by default (`u64::MAX`), and `POLARS_OOC_MEMORY_BUDGET_FRACTION` is parsed but never read anywhere.
- Workaround we're using: re-scan the source narrowly for the aggregate branch instead of reusing the same scan node, so there's no shared multiplexer to begin with.

issues.title: Allow explicit pruning of unused inputs in lazy horizontal concatenation
issues.body:
### Description

In Polars 2.0, `pl.concat(..., how="horizontal")` requires equal input heights. To preserve this invariant, projection pushdown retains at least one column from each input, even when none of its columns are selected downstream.

This prevents complete pruning of otherwise unused `LazyFrame` branches.

In modular, declarative pipelines, input heights may already be guaranteed equal by construction. Such pipelines commonly compose multiple `LazyFrame` branches horizontally to expose a wide schema, relying on downstream `.select()` operations to eliminate unnecessary computation.

[PR #27506](https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/pull/27506) introduced `POLARS_PROJECTION_PUSHDOWN_PRUNE_STRICT_HCONCAT_INPUTS=1`, which permits this optimisation. However, the setting is process-wide and is not exposed through the `pl.concat()` API.

### Minimal reproduction

```python
import polars as pl

lf_a = pl.LazyFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3]})
lf_b = pl.LazyFrame({"b": [4, 5, 6]})

q = pl.concat([lf_a, lf_b], how="horizontal").select("a")

print(pl.__version__)
print(q.explain())
```

On Polars 2.0.0, the default optimised logical plan retains both inputs, despite only selecting column `a`:

```text
simple π 1/1 ["a"]
  HCONCAT
    PLAN 0:
      DF ["a"]; PROJECT */1 COLUMNS
    PLAN 1:
      DF ["b"]; PROJECT */1 COLUMNS
  END HCONCAT
```

With `POLARS_PROJECTION_PUSHDOWN_PRUNE_STRICT_HCONCAT_INPUTS=1` set before running Python, the unused branch is eliminated:

```text
DF ["a"]; PROJECT */1 COLUMNS
```

### Performance impact

In my application, multiple lazy computation branches are horizontally composed into a `LazyFrame` exposing **72 columns**. Downstream consumers select only the columns they require, relying on projection pushdown to eliminate unused computation.

The following benchmarks illustrate the impact of retaining otherwise unused input branches when consumers request different subsets of those 72 available columns.

All three measurements use 20-million-row workloads:

| Downstream selection | Columns selected | Median time (of 7): default (s) | Median time (of 7): pruning (s) | Speedup | Plan nodes: default → pruning |
|----------------------|-----------------:|--------------------------------:|--------------------------------:|--------:|------------------------------:|
| A                    |    3 / 72 (4.2%) |                           1.283 |                           0.314 |    4.1× |                     854 → 465 |
| B                    |  30 / 72 (41.7%) |                           2.231 |                           1.235 |    1.8× |                     909 → 549 |
| C                    |  30 / 72 (41.7%) |                           1.343 |                           0.155 |    8.7× |                      768 → 66 |

Times are median execution times; plan-node counts are recorded by my application's plan-analysis instrumentation. These are application-level measurements, separate from the minimal reproduction above.

The performance difference depends not simply on the proportion of columns selected, but on which upstream branches are required to produce them. Notably, selections B and C request the same number of columns (different columns) yet benefit very differently from pruning.

For architectures that expose a broad lazy schema to downstream consumers, **the ability to eliminate entire unreferenced branches is essential to avoiding computation for outputs that are never requested**.

### Proposed enhancement

Expose an explicit, per-call opt-in for pruning unused inputs during strict horizontal concatenation, for example:

```python
pl.concat(
    [lf_a, lf_b],
    how="horizontal",
    prune_unselected=True,
)
```

The parameter name is illustrative.

This would preserve the existing height-validation guarantees by default, while allowing callers whose pipelines guarantee equal input heights by construction to explicitly opt into complete branch pruning.

The correctness trade-off is understood: eliminating an unused input also removes its runtime height validation, potentially suppressing a `ShapeError` if the caller's invariant is violated.

The objective is **not to weaken the default correctness guarantees**, but to make this existing optimiser capability explicit, discoverable, and locally configurable without relying on an undocumented process-wide environment variable.

### Related

- [PR #27506 — Fix lazy horizontal concat height validation after projection pushdown](https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/pull/27506)
- [Issue #27415 — Lazy horizontal concat with projection does not raise shape error for strict=True](https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/issues/27415)
- [Polars 2.0 migration guide](https://docs.pola.rs/releases/upgrade/2/)
issues.author: polite-clap-data-models

comments.body:
In other words - Producers can expose rich, wide `LazyFrame` schemas without requiring consumers to incur the computational cost of every contributing branch. Although projection pushdown already eliminates unused columns, strict horizontal concatenation retains height-witness columns from otherwise unselected inputs, potentially requiring substantial upstream computation.

**Complete branch pruning eliminates these otherwise unused branches entirely**, allowing consumers to benefit more fully from selecting only the columns they need. This optimisation is already available through an internal environment variable; the proposed enhancement would make it explicitly accessible at the `pl.concat()` call site.

Beyond the immediate performance gains, the broader value is architectural: this enables more centralised, expressive and reusable `LazyFrame`s capable of serving a wider range of consumers and use cases without unduly compromising execution efficiency.

issues.title: `scan_delta` filter on a struct column fails with "cast from `struct[1]` to `struct[5]`" when Delta stats cover only some of the struct's fields
issues.body:
### Checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pypi.org/project/polars/) of Polars.

### Reproducible example

```python
import tempfile

import polars as pl
from deltalake import write_deltalake

# 31 leading columns + a 5-field struct. Delta collects stats for the first 32
# leaf columns, so only field "a" of the struct gets stats.
df = pl.DataFrame(
    {f"c{i}": [0, 1] for i in range(31)}
    | {"flags": [{"a": a, "b": False, "c": False, "d": False, "e": False} for a in (True, False)]}
)

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as path:
    write_deltalake(path, df)
    print(pl.scan_delta(path).filter(~pl.col("flags").struct.field("a")).collect())
```


### Log output

```shell
File ".../polars/io/delta/_dataset.py", line 205, in to_dataset_scan
    _extract_table_statistics_from_delta_add_actions(
  File ".../polars/io/delta/_utils.py", line 160, in _extract_table_statistics_from_delta_add_actions
    col_nc.cast(nc_dtype) if col_nc is not None else null_col(nc_dtype)
  File ".../polars/series/series.py", line 4795, in cast
polars.exceptions.InvalidOperationError: cast from `struct[1]` to `struct[5]` failed in column 'flags': structs do not have the same number of fields: 1 vs 5

Ensure that any output struct has the same number of fields as the input, and that all struct field names in the output are present in the input.
Use `strict=False` to force the cast, and Polars will select the first n fields from the struct.
```

```shell
1
61 verbose_fail.log
total memory: 7.841 GiB (8419655680 bytes)
_init_credential_provider_builder(): credential_provider_init = None
async thread count: 2
blocking thread count: 512
python scan_resolve_threadpool threads: 128
python scan_resolve_threadpool threads: 128
expand_datasets(): python[DeltaDataset]: limit: None, project: all
DeltaDataset: to_dataset_scan(): version: None, limit: None, projection: None, filter_columns: ['flags'], use_pyarrow: False
DeltaDataset: to_dataset_scan(): begin path expansion
DeltaDataset: to_dataset_scan(): native scan_parquet(): num_files: 1, path expansion time: 0.001s
Traceback (most recent call last):
polars.exceptions.InvalidOperationError: cast from `struct[1]` to `struct[5]` failed in column 'flags': structs do not have the same number of fields: 1 vs 5

Ensure that any output struct has the same number of fields as the input, and that all struct field names in the output are present in the input.
Use `strict=False` to force the cast, and Polars will select the first n fields from the struct.
```

### Issue description

By default, Delta writers collect file statistics only for the first 32 leaf columns (`delta.dataSkippingNumIndexedCols`). When a struct column straddles that limit, the `null_count`/`min`/`max` stats structs in the add actions contain only the indexed subset of the struct's fields. `_extract_table_statistics_from_delta_add_actions` then casts them to the full column dtype, and the strict struct cast fails on the field-count mismatch.

Changing the number of leading columns in the example shows the boundary:

| leading columns | struct fields with stats | result |
|---|---|---|
| ≤ 27 | 5 of 5 | ok |
| 28–31 | 4 … 1 of 5 | `InvalidOperationError` |
| ≥ 32 | 0 of 5 | ok (stats column absent, `null_col` used) |

Only predicates that reference the struct column trigger this, because only those columns go into `filter_columns`. Blocking predicate pushdown (e.g. wrapping the predicate in `map_batches`) avoids the error.

This is a regression: the example runs fine on polars 1.44.2. The struct stats cast was introduced in #27887 and is still present on `main`. The `min`/`max` casts a few lines below (`col_min.cast(dtype)`, `col_max.cast(dtype)`) will hit the same mismatch.


### Expected behavior

The query returns the matching row. Struct fields without stats should be filled with nulls by name (i.e. "unknown", so no file skipping on those fields) instead of being strictly cast.


### Installed versions

<details>

```
- polars 2.0.0
- deltalake 1.6.6
- Python 3.13, Linux x86_64
```

</details>

issues.title: Consistent random-access slices over a LazyFrame (for an interactive data viewer)
issues.body:
### Context

I maintain [larray-editor](https://github.com/larray-project/larray-editor), a GUI viewer for (among many other objects) Polars objects and large Parquet files. It shows ~40 rows at a time and lets users scroll anywhere in the result, including jumping to the middle. The metric I care most about is the time to display the first rows.

For LazyFrames, each slice is fetched separately with `lf[start:stop].collect()`. For scans, filters and element-wise operations, this seems both correct and very fast thanks to slice pushdown. But because each slice comes from a separate execution, when the order of the result is not defined (slices of e.g. a `group_by` without `maintain_order=True`, `unique` or `join`) are often inconsistent:

```python
import numpy as np
import polars as pl

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 2_000_000
lf = pl.LazyFrame({'k': rng.integers(0, 5000, n), 'v': rng.random(n)})
query = lf.group_by('k').agg(pl.col('v').sum())

# what my viewer does: fetch each slice separately (usually less than 1000 rows at a time,
# but 1000 makes the problem more obvious)
first_slice = query[0:1000].collect()
second_slice = query[1000:2000].collect()
displayed = pl.concat([first_slice, second_slice])

num_displayed_keys = displayed['k'].n_unique()
print(f"{num_displayed_keys} distinct keys among the first 2000 rows displayed")
# prints about 1800 (it varies between runs) instead of 2000: some groups are displayed
# twice and others not at all
```

This is expected given the documented semantics, so this is *not* a bug report. Filtering on a `with_row_index()` instead of slicing does not help either, since the index is assigned during each execution.

### What I found so far (with the help of Claude Opus 5.5)

- Materializing the entire result once (`execute()` or `collect()`) then slice it makes the slices consistent, but the first rows then take as long as the whole query. `collect_batches()` streams (its first batch arrives quickly whatever the file size), but the query then runs to completion and it gives no random access to the middle. Displaying larger-than-RAM datasets through `scan_*` is the reason I display lazy frames in the first place, so waiting for the whole result is not an option.
- Setting `maintain_order=True` on `group_by`, `unique` and `sort`, and `maintain_order='left'` on `join`, makes the slices consistent in my tests. `explain()` shows this setting, except for joins (the private `NodeTraverser` does show it for joins). I found no supported way to turn it on for an existing query: editing every `maintain_order` in the plan's JSON serialization works, but that format is deprecated and embeds in-memory data.
- To keep the viewer responsive, I plan to fetch slices with `collect(background=True)`, letting users cancel slow queries, instead of trying to predict how long a query will take.

### Questions

1. Is the row order of scans, `filter` and element-wise operations guaranteed to be the same across executions, now and going forward (e.g. with multi-threaded scans)? `filter` documents it, but I found nothing explicit for scans.
2. Is it guaranteed that a query whose operations all maintain order (as above) gives the same rows in the same order on each execution?
3. Is there (or could there be) a stable way to know whether the output order of a query is defined, so that a viewer can slice when it is and materialize the result once when it is not?
4. Is there (or could there be) a supported way to make an existing query maintain order everywhere, e.g. an engine option? Besides my use case, I know several users who would rather keep their row order everywhere and lose some performance than the opposite.
5. Is there (or could there be) a way to get random-access slices of a *single* execution without waiting for the whole result? For example a `QueryResult` (from `execute()`) which fills progressively and can be sliced while it does, or a way to stop `collect_batches()` (its docstring mentions `stop`, but I could not find it on the returned object).
6. Background mode (`collect(background=True)`) is marked unstable. Is it meant to stay?

I *am* well aware that displaying some queries "live" makes no sense: some could run for days before producing their first row. But it has a lot of value for the queries where it does make sense, and I would like a way to make it work for those and to tell them apart. Any advice on the best approach would be very welcome.

### Related

- narwhals-dev/narwhals#2389, where this ordering problem was pointed out to me.
- #27694 (expression determinism classification), which could help with question 3.

### Environment

Polars 2.0.0, Python 3.13, Windows 11

comments.body:
1. Scans are ordered if their order is observed. It doesn't make any sense to talk about the order of element-wise operations.
2. If all operations are deterministic in terms of order then yes the query is deterministic. Note that some things fundamentally drop the order (e.g. a `sum` or the input to a non-stable `sort`) so those can be transformed to non-order-preserving by the optimizer. But outside of float determinism this shouldn't affect you.
3. Not yet.
4. Not yet.
5. I don't understand the question. 
6. I don't know right now, does `collect_async` do what you want?

issues.title: Windows: access violation in bundled mimalloc 3.3.2 (`_mi_subproc` null `tld`), fixed upstream in mimalloc 3.4.1
issues.body:
### Checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pypi.org/project/polars/) of Polars.
  Confirmed on 1.44.1. Not run on 1.44.2 / 2.0.0, but both lock the same `libmimalloc-sys 0.1.49` (bundled mimalloc 3.3.2) per their `Cargo.lock`, and so does `main` today.

### Reproducible example

There is no standalone reproducer: this is a thread-teardown race inside the allocator, so it only shows up in a long-lived process that keeps creating and retiring worker threads that touch Polars. Our case is a Streamlit server (script-runner threads plus `ThreadPoolExecutor` workers) doing ordinary Polars work (`scan_parquet`, `collect`, `cast`, `DataFrame.__setstate__` from cache hits, roughly 90 such calls per second while pages build). Replaying the same reads and unpickles in a bare process (tens of thousands of iterations) never crashed.

The crashing call is whatever happens to allocate at the wrong moment, e.g.:

```python
df.with_columns(pl.col("x").cast(pl.Utf8))
```

### Log output

```shell
Windows fatal exception: access violation

Current thread 0x00001ac4 [ScriptRunner.scriptThread] (most recent call first):
  File ".venv\Lib\site-packages\polars\datatypes\classes.py", line 302 in to_dtype_expr
  File ".venv\Lib\site-packages\polars\datatypes\_parse.py", line 49 in parse_into_datatype_expr
  File ".venv\Lib\site-packages\polars\expr\expr.py", line 2227 in cast
  File "<app>", ... (application frames)
  File ".venv\Lib\site-packages\streamlit\runtime\scriptrunner\script_runner.py", line 399 in _run_script_thread
  File "...\Lib\threading.py", line 1044 in _bootstrap
```

Windows Error Reporting, every occurrence on the official 1.44.1 `win_amd64` wheel:

```
Faulting module: _polars_runtime.pyd   Exception code: 0xc0000005   Offset: 0x00000000085dc347
Access violation reading address 0x0000000000000018
```

### Issue description

**Summary:** the Windows wheels bundle mimalloc 3.3.2 (via `mimalloc 0.1.52` → `libmimalloc-sys 0.1.49`, v3 enabled on Windows since #27111 / #27395). mimalloc 3.3.x has a known null dereference in `_mi_subproc()` when a thread re-enters the allocator after `_mi_thread_done`. mimalloc fixed it in **v3.4.1** (microsoft/mimalloc#1289, report microsoft/mimalloc#1287). The Rust wrapper has not released it yet: purpleprotocol/mimalloc_rust#169 ("Update mimalloc to v2.4.5 and v3.4.5") has been open since 2026-07-23.

**What we saw:** 54 `access violation` crashes between 2026-08-26 and 2026-09-22 in one long-running Streamlit process on Windows 11, 1–4 per day. All of them were on non-main threads, and all were inside Polars frames, with very different entry points (`scan_parquet` 15, `collect` 15, `columns` 15, `cast`, unpickling). On the current build every crash faulted at the same instruction, `_polars_runtime.pyd+0x85dc347`, reading address `0x18`.

**Root cause (from three minidumps and a disassembly of the official 1.44.1 wheel):**

```
+85dc306  mov rcx,[_mi_theap_default_slot]     ; TlsAlloc slot
+85dc30d  mov rdx,gs:[rcx*8]                   ; TEB slot
+85dc31d  cmp rcx,0x2F0                        ; MI_TLS_EXPANSION_SLOT branch
+85dc332  mov rdx,[rdx+rax*8]                  ; theap = TlsExpansionSlots[idx]
+85dc339  jne +344                             ; theap != NULL ?
+85dc33b  lea rbx,[subproc_main]               ;   NULL -> _mi_subproc_main()
+85dc344  mov rax,[rdx]                        ; rax = theap->tld
+85dc347  mov rbx,[rax+0x18]                   ; <-- fault: tld->subproc with tld == NULL
```

That is mimalloc 3.3.2 `src/init.c` `_mi_subproc()`:

```c
mi_theap_t* theap = _mi_theap_default();
if (theap == NULL) { return _mi_subproc_main(); }
else { return theap->tld->subproc; }   // theap->tld == NULL -> read of [0x18]
```

In all three dumps `theap != NULL && theap->tld == NULL`. The only writer of `theap->tld = NULL` is `_mi_theap_free()`. mimalloc 3.4.1 changed the check to `if (theap == NULL || theap->tld == NULL)`. Later releases extend the guard (microsoft/mimalloc#1391) and fix a 3.5.2 regression in 3.5.3.

**Verification:** we rebuilt `py-1.44.1` with only this change:

```toml
[patch.crates-io]
libmimalloc-sys = { git = "https://github.com/xonatius/mimalloc_rust", rev = "6d4c41bb10c6d9da1d1b6f07b38c4cc051667f11" }  # head of mimalloc_rust#169, mimalloc 3.4.5
```

Decoding the rebuilt `_polars_runtime.pyd` shows all 15 inlined `_mi_subproc` sites now take the `tld == NULL` branch (unguarded 15 → 0). The process ran on that build from 2026-09-22 to 2026-10-09 (17 days) with no access violation, against 54 in the 4 weeks before. Then a dependency re-sync silently reinstalled the PyPI wheel for 3 days, also without a crash, before we restored the patched build. The crash rate had already fallen in the last stretch before the patch (13 crashes from 09-12 to 09-22), so a few clean weeks are consistent with the fix but do not prove it. The real evidence is the instruction-level match and the upstream fix.

Possibly related open issues with the same Windows `0xc0000005` shape: #26617 (long-lived worker, "needs repro"), #23142, and #28961 (Windows CI access violations, handled by skipping tests).

**Ask:** pick up a `libmimalloc-sys` that bundles mimalloc ≥ 3.4.1 (ideally ≥ 3.5.3) as soon as one is released. Until then, a `[patch.crates-io]` like the one above (or a vendored one-line guard) would stop these crashes for Windows users. A nudge on purpleprotocol/mimalloc_rust#169 from the Polars side would probably help as well.

### Expected behavior

issues.title: Elementwise check on `join` expressions is too restrictive
issues.body:
### Checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pypi.org/project/polars/) of Polars.

### Reproducible example

All following expressions results in `InvalidOperationError: All join key expressions must be elementwise.`

```py
df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [1,2,3,4]})

df.join(df, left_on="a", right_on=pl.int_range(pl.len()))
df.join(df, left_on="a", right_on=pl.col("a") * pl.len())
df.join(df, left_on="a", right_on=pl.col("a").cum_count())
df.join(df, left_on="a", right_on=pl.col("a").shift());
```

### Log output

_No response_

### Issue description

Since https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/pull/17517, the expressions allowed in `join` clauses have a check in place to ensure that all rows in both dataframes will be assigned a value. This check is made with the function `is_streamable`. But this checks is currently too restrictive, marking as invalid expressions that should be.

This is especially inconvenient because it makes it impossible to use the implicit row index of a dataframe in those expressions, forcing us to add it with `with_row_index()` and drop it at the end with `.drop("index")`.

### Expected behavior

The check should better discriminate between valid and invalid expressions.

comments.body:
I think this is a good point, and one could do a tighter job of classifying expressions.

Before embarking on this for the purpose of join keys, we should decide what "valid" join keys look like.

Your example shows four different styles of expression for the right join key. These are not trivial to classify correctly. Note that `pl.len()` is a reduction for which we need to know that the result will _symbolically_ produce something that, when used, will produce a correct-length join key. Consider with a different reduction `pl.col("a").count()`. This happens to produce the same value as `pl.len()` iff `a` contains no nulls. Both would be usable in the case `a * reduced_value` (your second example). But only `len` is guaranteed usable for your first example.

But if there are no non-null values - you hit the ShapeError bug.

If we can modify the UDF, we can get a typed dict from a DataFrame, and set the correct `return_dtype`:

```python
def return_dict(s):
    result = {"a": "1", "b": "two"}
    return pl.DataFrame(result).cast(schema).to_struct().item()
    
schema = {"a": pl.Int64, "b": pl.String}
    
df = pl.DataFrame({"x": 1})
```

```python
df.with_columns(y = pl.all().map_elements(return_dict, return_dtype=pl.Struct(schema)))
# shape: (1, 2)
# ┌─────┬───────────┐
# │ x   ┆ y         │
# │ --- ┆ ---       │
# │ i64 ┆ struct[2] │
# ╞═════╪═══════════╡
# │ 1   ┆ {1,"two"} │
# └─────┴───────────┘
```

```python
(pl.DataFrame({"x": [None]})
   .with_columns(y = pl.all().map_elements(return_dict, return_dtype=pl.Struct(schema)))
) 
# shape: (1, 2)
# ┌──────┬─────────────┐
# │ x    ┆ y           │
# │ ---  ┆ ---         │
# │ null ┆ struct[2]   │
# ╞══════╪═════════════╡
# │ null ┆ {null,null} │
# └──────┴─────────────┘
```

But I'm not sure if this is the way this is supposed to be done?
comments.author: cmdlineluser

comments.body:
I would be very surprised if this was the intended way. But it's good to have this as a workaround. 

@janikkokot So putting the schema in fields rather than a dict works to circumvent this problem?
comments.author: Baukebrenninkmeijer

comments.body:
@cmdlineluser 
```python
df.with_columns(
    pl.struct(
        pl.col('text_column')
          .str.extract(r'\{([^}]+)\}')
          .str.extract(rf'{name}=([^,}}]+)')
          .cast(dtype, strict=False)
          .alias(name) 
        for name, dtype in schema.items()
    )
)
```
This works flawlessly, thanks for suggesting it!

comments.body:
This has come up before. Polars tries to guess the orientation by the schema and the dimensions of the data. But if `n_cols == n_rows`, Polars doesn't know and defaults to column representation, as this is a much more efficient way of reading the data.

The immediate fix is to use `orient="row"` to stop Polars from guessing.

This is a sharp edge that I've run into many times before, but I don't really know how to fix this nicely. A better error message is probably warranted. at least.

EDIT: I think I misread your initial example. Slicing the input gives different results, which _is_ weird...
